To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
WM training does not transfer to untrained WM tasks and to closely related abilities.
WM training did not improve performance in untrained, structually different WM tasks and closely related abilities.
the training interventions did not enhance WM capacity or the WM mechanisms assumed underlie transfer.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying transfer of training effects and provides evidence that WM training may be less effective than assumed.
the question whether WM training is effective in enhancing the cognitive abilities beyond WM.
the question whether WM training can improve WM capacity and WM processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
WM training does not transfer to any other cognitive abilities.
WM training is not effective to improve cognitive performance in young adults.
the WM training did not work, at least not for the sample investigated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
WM training is not a promising tool to improve WM capacity, WM efficiency, or other closely related cognitive abilities.
WM updating and WM binding training did not improve WM performance and transfer.
the WM training effects are not as strong and reliable as previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the absence of training-induced improvements in the transfer tasks cannot be attributed to a lack of statistical power, practice effects, or task correlations.
the effectiveness of WM training depends on the training design, which should consider not only the training tasks but also the training procedures.
